chapters.title: Two paths toward a meeting
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: Come, sit by the fire. A woman has reached the meeting place before her travelling companion. Across the water, the path is still empty. She lifts her bundle: if she leaves now, she can reach home before dark. But if her companion arrives after she has gone, there will be nobody to meet her. The bundle settles against her shoulder. She takes a step, then looks once more toward the bend.

questions.label: Why is she thinking of leaving?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: Home is still a walk away, and the light is going. If she leaves, she can reach it before dark. If she stays, someone may find her waiting.

questions.label: Does this tell my ancestor's journey?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: No ancestor's journey is established here. A fragment can guide curiosity about movement and encounters; it cannot establish anyone's biography.

chapters.title: A region of overlapping lives
chapters.narration: Before 1900, trade linked pastoral Maasai and predominantly agricultural Kikuyu communities around Kiambu; settlement and economic activity overlapped.

choices.label: Stay with the one who waits
Find the one who is late

chapters.title: What a traveller carries onward
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: She chooses to put the bundle down. For a while there is only the water and the fire. Then the missing woman comes round the bend, holding her gourd close. 'I thought you would have gone.' The waiting woman moves her bundle aside. 'I nearly did.' They sit in the space it leaves. When they rise, the path home is darker, but neither follows it alone.

questions.label: What could I ask a relative next?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: You could ask which places or journeys they remember, and whose account each detail comes from. Their answers would remain personal accounts unless separately supported.

chapters.title: A promise still walking
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: On the far side of the water, the late woman is still walking. The path has taken longer than she planned, and the gourd she carries grows heavier with every step. The light is going. If she turns back now, she can send word tomorrow, and nobody will blame her. But a message cannot sit beside someone at dusk. She chooses to keep walking, holding the gourd close, not knowing whether anyone is still there. At the bend she stops. A bundle has been set down by the water, and beside it, a woman is waiting.

questions.label: What could I ask about a journey someone made?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: You could ask what made the journey long, who waited at the other end, and whether word was ever sent ahead. Their answers would remain personal accounts unless separately supported.

sources.title: John Overton (1988): The Origins of the Kikuyu Land Problem

chapters.title: A household's small decisions
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: Come closer to the fire. A woman tips her flour gourd and listens. Less than she thought. At home, a small portion still waits beside the hearth. She could add it to the gourd and arrive with the full load she promised. Instead she leaves that portion where it is. Now she must carry a different weight to the meeting: the words that will explain the shortfall.

questions.label: Why didn't she bring the rest?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: She left a portion at home. Bringing it would fill the promised gourd, but empty that place beside her own hearth. She is carrying the cost of that choice to the meeting.

questions.label: What do museums record about gourds?
questions.answer: A National Museums of Kenya exhibit describes a Maasai gourd used for milk or blood and smoked inside with oloirien wood. This museum example does not establish the design of every vessel used in the 1850s.

choices.label: Follow the one who brought less
Wait with the one who expected more

chapters.title: The agreement belongs to the women
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: At the water, she opens the gourd before the other woman can offer hers. 'This is all I could bring.' She keeps her hands beside it, waiting to be turned away. The other woman draws her own bundle back. Then she separates a smaller share and sets it between them. 'Then let us begin with what is here.' They choose the smaller exchange together. Back at the hearth, the woman sets her gourd beside the portion she left. Neither is full. Together, they are enough for tonight.

questions.label: Is this exchange a historical custom?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: This particular exchange and its terms are invented. A documented regional trade relationship does not prove this bargain or a universal custom.

chapters.title: The one who expected more
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: The other woman reached the water first, her own share wrapped and ready. She has counted on the flour; at home, tonight's meal was planned around it. When the gourd arrives, she can see how lightly it is carried before a word is spoken. She could draw her share back and walk home, having lost nothing but an afternoon. She could ask for what was promised. Instead she watches the woman's hands resting beside the gourd, as if waiting to be turned away. She chooses to make the exchange smaller rather than let it end. 'Then let us begin with what is here.'

questions.label: What did accepting less cost her?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: In this telling, a smaller share means a smaller meal at home tonight. The scene invents that cost to show her choice; it is not a record of any household's portions or of a custom.

chapters.title: Begin with the water
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: Come, sit where the fire catches the water. A woman brings a younger traveller to the bank she remembers. 'Here,' she says. But the traveller points to the next bend. 'You said the path opened beside the reeds.' The woman looks at the water, then at the bundle she has set down. She had promised to show a place. Now she is no longer sure she has found it.

questions.label: Why does finding this place matter?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: She promised to show the traveller a place she remembers. The uncertainty is not only about the bend. It is whether she can share what that place meant to her.

questions.label: Is this the exact historical riverbank?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: The painted bank is a reconstruction. It does not locate a particular household, meeting or ancestor.

chapters.title: A name with limits
chapters.narration: Nairobi's name is commonly traced to a Maa phrase meaning cool waters.

questions.label: What does Enkare Nairobi mean?
questions.answer: Nairobi's name is commonly traced to a Maa phrase meaning cool waters. Spelling and pronunciation still need review by a Maa speaker.

chapters.title: A place can hold another question
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: She chooses not to pretend. 'I remember the water. I may have the bend wrong.' She lifts the bundle and makes room for the traveller beside her. Instead of pointing, she describes the sound she remembers. The traveller closes her eyes to listen. The telling passes from one voice to another while the water keeps moving. Much later, by a river with a city beyond it, another visitor pauses to listen before choosing where to stand.

questions.label: What could I ask about a remembered place?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: Ask what the place was called, who used that name, and whether there is a photograph, map or personal account to compare. A remembered name alone cannot verify ancestry.

chapters.title: The one who was shown
chapters.narration: Imagined scene: The younger traveller came to be shown a place, and she was sure of the reeds. Now she watches the older woman look from the water to the bundle and back, and understands that the bend may have moved, or the memory has. She could press: 'You said the reeds.' She could walk ahead to prove it. Instead she chooses a different question. 'What did it sound like?' The older woman closes her eyes to answer. Years from now, the traveller will remember that sound better than any bend, and she will be the one who is not quite sure where it was.

questions.label: What could I ask someone who remembers a place?
questions.answer: Imagined scene: Ask what it sounded, smelled or looked like, and who else went there. A vivid memory can hold true detail even when its exact location is uncertain; it remains a personal account unless other evidence supports it.
